objectives.statement: The code of conduct is approved by the chief executive or a founder. It covers ethical behaviour, acceptable use, conflicts of interest, confidentiality and what happens on a breach, and requires acknowledgement at hire and every year.
Each employee and contractor who joined in the period acknowledged the code by their start date, with a record that names them and is dated.
Everyone on the staff list acknowledged the current version within the last 12 months. Each missing acknowledgement was chased and, where it stayed open, passed to the disciplinary process.
Each breach of the code was recorded with the date raised, what happened, who decided and the action taken, and was closed. Where there were none, a dated nil return covers the period.

The disciplinary procedure is approved by the chief executive. It sets the range of sanctions from warning to dismissal, who decides, how security breaches are handled, the right to respond and how records are kept.
The code of conduct that staff acknowledged referred to the disciplinary procedure, so each person had been told the consequence before any breach.
Each disciplinary case in the period followed the steps of the procedure, with the rule broken, the steps taken, the outcome and the dates recorded, or a dated nil note from HR covers the period.
Each recorded breach of security policy in the period was passed to the procedure, and comparable breaches received comparable outcomes.
Case records were kept by HR with access limited to the people handling each case, together with the decision and its basis.

A current organization chart shows each role, its reporting line and the security owner, and role descriptions for the security lead, control owners and others with compliance duties state purpose, duties, authority and reporting line.
The security lead reported to someone able to act on the issues raised, without a conflict of interest with the work security oversees.
Leadership reviewed the structure and reporting lines in the last 12 months and after each reorganization, and recorded the changes agreed and who owns them.
On the date tested, the chart matched the current staff, and each role with security duties was held by a current member of staff.
A written appointment, approved by the chief executive or the board, names the security officer and a deputy, with duties, authority, budget, escalation path and a reporting line to leadership.

The named officer held the role throughout the period. Each change of officer or deputy was recorded with a new appointment from the date it took effect, and where a regulator requires it, the role sat outside IT operations.
The security officer briefed leadership in writing each quarter on risks, incidents, audit findings and open actions, and set out the decisions asked for.
Decisions the officer asked for and items they escalated were answered by leadership and followed through.

Approved terms of reference name the body that oversees security, how often it meets, at least once a year, and what it reviews: security posture, material incidents, risk results and remediation progress.
The membership record lists each member with role and start date, and shows which members are independent of day to day management.
The body met as often as its terms set during the period, and each meeting worked from a written security pack covering posture, material incidents, risk results and remediation progress.
Minutes show members questioned the security information and recorded their decisions, including any resourcing or risk acceptance decisions, with follow up actions and owners.
Follow up actions from each meeting were reported back at a later meeting and either closed or carried forward with a reason.

An approved procedure sets a management review at least each quarter with the security lead and managers who can commit resources, lists the inputs to the yearly executive review, and states how actions are recorded and escalated.

A management review took place each quarter of the period with the security lead and managers able to commit resources, and covered control health, open findings, incidents, risk changes and remediation progress.
In the last 12 months the executive team judged whether the program still fits the business and works, using the set inputs, and recorded its decisions on improvements, changes and resources.
Each action raised had a named owner and due date and was tracked to closure, and any still open was carried to the next review rather than closed without a record.
Items left open across two reviews in a row were escalated to the oversight body.

The roles document requires every control to have one named person as owner, with the authority that owner holds to act, and sets that ownership is reviewed every year and on each leaver or role change.
At the test date every control in scope had exactly one owner, each owner was a current member of staff, and controls that need judgement were owned by a person rather than a team inbox.
When an owner left or changed role in the period, their controls moved to a new named owner by the leaving date, with the date and reason recorded.
The ownership mapping was reviewed in the last 12 months, and owners asked could say which controls they own and what they may do to act on them.
The system description is approved and current for the report date. It sets out the services, the system boundary, infrastructure, software, people, procedures, data, third parties and key controls.
Each commitment made to customers, such as uptime, encryption and breach notice, and each legal, regulatory and contractual requirement, is listed with the system requirement that meets it.
For each third party the system depends on, the description states which controls that party operates and which stay with the company.
The description was reviewed in the last 12 months and after each material change, and when compared with what is deployed, no in scope system, data store or supplier was missing.
The risk method is written and approved by leadership. It sets the scoring scales, the level of risk that may be accepted and by whom, and when assessments are repeated.
The assessment covered the whole declared scope: each in scope service, asset group and critical supplier appears against a risk or a recorded conclusion that none is significant.
Every risk had an owner, likelihood and impact on the approved scale, and a result compared with the acceptance level.
The assessment was done in the last 12 months and again after each significant change.
Leadership reviewed and signed the results, and the results drove the treatment plan and the applicability decisions.

The risk method sets what the register holds for each risk: description, category, owner, inherent rating, mitigating controls, residual rating, a treatment of accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid, and who may approve an acceptance.
Every risk on the register had a named owner, likelihood, impact, score, treatment decision and date of last review, and each mitigated risk was linked to the controls that reduce it.
The register was reviewed at each management review in the period, and each rating change was recorded with its date.
Each risk accepted in the period was approved at the set level by someone other than the person who asked, with a reason and an expiry or next review date.

The risk policy states that each mitigated risk gets a treatment plan approved by its risk owner, that a risk is rated again only once treatment is shown to be in place, and that the owner accepts the remaining risk in writing.
Each risk chosen for mitigation had planned actions with an accountable owner, a target date and an expected residual rating, and its risk owner approved the plan.
Each treatment action closed in the period had proof of the change attached, such as a screenshot, ticket or setting change, not a status update alone.
Each risk was rated again only after its treatment was shown to be in place. The risk owner then accepted the remaining risk in writing, or sent it back where it stayed above the acceptance level.
Treatment actions past their due date were reported at management review with a new date or a decision.

The risk method requires the annual assessment to cover fraud and insider misuse, looking at incentive, opportunity and how a person might justify it, and to consider leaders overriding controls by name.

The last annual assessment recorded fraud risks such as payment fraud, data theft by staff and management override, each with a score and a treatment, with a conclusion recorded even where the risk was low.
Each fraud risk was linked to mitigating controls such as least privilege, separation of duties, logging or independent review.
Each action chosen for a fraud risk was completed by its owner with proof that the change is live, or the risk was accepted with a recorded approval.

The risk method lists the events that force a review outside the annual cycle, such as a new subprocessor touching customer data, a major architecture or hosting change, a new data type or country, or a reorganization, and names who runs it.
Each trigger event in the period had a risk review recorded against it, with the date, the change, the risks added or rescored and who took part, or a dated nil note covers the period.
Each triggered review was finished before the change went live, and for projects that change systems, data, sites or suppliers it was held at the planning stage.
New or changed risks found by triggered reviews were entered in the register with an owner, a score and a treatment decision.
The trigger list was reviewed in the last 12 months and updated where the business had changed.

The risk method requires each risk to name the controls that reduce it, flags risks with no control and controls tied to no risk, and requires a signed acceptance by the risk owner for any risk left unmitigated.
Every treated risk in the register was linked to at least one control, and the status of each linked control was shown.
Each risk with no mitigating control carried an acceptance decision signed by its risk owner.
Each control tied to no listed risk was flagged and reviewed, and the review recorded whether a risk was missing from the register or the control was not needed.
The mapping was revisited each quarter and whenever a control was disabled or a risk was added, so no risk was left relying only on a disabled control.

The in scope system list names each production system, its owner and the access, change, backup and monitoring controls over it, and each system left out of scope has a recorded reason and any compensating control.
The system list was complete when compared with billing, the identity provider and the asset inventory, including systems adopted informally or through an acquisition.
A dated review in the last 12 months checked every listed system against the access, change and operations controls, and each gap found was raised as a task with an owner.
Each coverage gap was closed by its due date, or covered by an approved compensating control.

The top level security policy is approved by top management, or by the board where a regulator requires it. It states the security objectives or how they are set, and commits to meeting legal, regulatory and contractual duties and to improving.

A current policy exists for each required topic: security, access, change, incidents, continuity and recovery, suppliers, cloud use, data handling, acceptable use with clear desk and screen, remote working and secure development.
Each policy carries an owner, version, approval date and next review date, and its current version was approved by its accountable manager through the recorded approval step.
The current version of each policy was available to all staff at a known location during the period, and the top level policy was shared with customers or other parties that needed it.

The document control procedure is approved and requires every policy to be reviewed at least once a year and after a material change, through the recorded approval step, with the reviewer, date and outcome kept.
Every published policy was reviewed within the last 12 months, and each record names the reviewer, the review date and the outcome, including where the outcome was no change.
Each review compared the policy with how the organization actually works, and every gap found was corrected in the policy or raised as a deficiency with an owner.
Changed policies were re approved by their accountable owner through the documented approval step rather than edited in place, and superseded versions were kept so the history can be traced.
After each material change to the business or environment in the period, the policies it affected were reviewed without waiting for the annual cycle.

The measurement plan is approved. It says which controls are checked automatically and how often, how systems that cannot be connected are checked, who receives a failure and the time allowed to fix it.
Checks ran on their set schedule across the whole period, and each result was kept with its date and time, so the operating history has no unexplained gaps.
Each failed check was raised to the named control owner and fixed within the set time, with the date found, the fix and the date closed recorded.
Checks that failed repeatedly were reviewed for a design weakness instead of being closed one occurrence at a time, and each review led to a recorded change or decision.
Periods when monitoring itself was not running were recorded with their dates, the cause and what was done to cover the gap.
A written requirement sets an independent penetration test at least once a year and after a major architecture change, the minimum scope, and the time allowed to fix findings by severity.
Before each test, the targets, dates, allowed test types, contacts and the way to stop the test in an emergency were agreed in writing and signed by the system owner and the tester.

A tester independent of the team running the systems tested in the last 12 months, covering internet facing applications and infrastructure, plus the internal network where systems run on premises or handle card data, with exclusions stated.
Each finding was recorded with an owner and fixed within the time set for its severity, or accepted with a recorded approval.
Each high and critical finding was retested, and the tester's retest letter or report confirms it was fixed.

The approved internal audit program sets what is audited and how often, based on importance and earlier results, the methods and criteria used, who plans, performs and reports each audit, and how auditors stay independent.

In the last 12 months and before the external audit, an internal audit covered the whole security program, management processes as well as controls, and recorded scope, criteria, dates, evidence examined and findings.
Each area was audited by someone who did not own or operate the controls in it, or by an outside reviewer.
Results went to the managers responsible and to management review, and each finding became an owned, dated remediation action tracked to closure.

An approved procedure requires every finding from audits, tests, monitoring, incidents and complaints to go into one tracker. It sets due dates by severity, the closure proof needed, and when overdue items are escalated.
Every deficiency found in the period was logged with its source, date found, owner, severity, root cause and due date, including those raised by internal audit and by incidents.
The owner and leadership were told of each deficiency soon after it was found, with the due date it was given.

Each deficiency was closed by its severity due date with proof attached rather than the owner's word alone, and significant ones were checked again after a set period to confirm the problem had not returned.
Deficiencies past their due date were reported at management review. Where the cause pointed to a wider gap, other systems were checked and the policy, procedure or control was changed.
A register lists every legal, regulatory, contractual and certification obligation that applies, each with its source, what it requires, a named owner and a review date.
Each obligation in the register was mapped to the controls that meet it, and each obligation with no control was raised as a gap with an owner.
The register was complete. Customer contracts with security terms, the laws of each country served and each certification held all appeared in it.
The register was reviewed in the last 12 months and whenever a new market was entered or a contract with new requirements was signed, with the date, reviewer, sources checked and changes made.
The current approved version of each policy is published, with its date, where all staff can read it without asking. Staff must acknowledge the policies at hire and after each material change.
Throughout the period each policy on the portal was the latest approved version.
Every person on the staff list acknowledged the current policies at hire and after each material change, recorded per person, per policy and with the date.
Each material policy change in the period was announced to staff rather than left for them to notice.
Outstanding acknowledgements were followed up, and people who still had not acknowledged were escalated.
A security reporting channel, such as a security address or form, is published for staff and customers. It names who reads it and the expected response time, and the incident plan points to it.
Staff were told about the channel at onboarding and in training, and the security page and security.txt pointed to a monitored address throughout the period.
Every report received in the period was logged with the date, sender, summary, triage decision and date closed, or a dated nil return was kept.
Each report was answered within the stated response time and routed into incident triage, and each one judged to be an incident appears in the incident register.

The approved staff policy describes a confidential reporting channel. It says how to report, that reports may be anonymous, who receives and investigates them, who is kept out of a report about themselves, and that retaliation is banned.
All staff were told about the channel and the ban on retaliation through the policies they acknowledged.
Each report in the period was logged without names, with its category, investigation steps, outcome and date closed, or the person who receives reports kept a dated nil return.
No report was handled by a person it concerned, and reports about a manager were taken outside that reporting line.
The number and categories of reports were shared with the oversight body.
Terms of service, service levels, a security page and a privacy notice are published and dated, and together state what customers are promised on security, uptime and privacy.
The commitments in the system description are the same as those published to customers, with nothing promised in one and missing from the other.
In the last 12 months, and after each material change to the service, the security lead compared each promise with how the system really works and named the control or setting that meets it.
Each promise that practice did not meet was resolved by changing the practice or correcting the published text, and the change was recorded.
Each change to a committed term in the period was approved before it was published, and the approval was recorded.

The standard customer agreement states the breach notice timeframe, what customers are told and who is told, and contracts that differ are recorded. The approved incident plan applies the shortest timeframe and names who decides and who sends the notice.
Throughout the period the incident plan in use matched the timeframes in the customer contracts, and the notice template it holds covered what the contracts require customers to be told.
For each security incident in the period, the customer notice decision was recorded with who made it and when, including decisions not to notify.
Each customer notice that was required was sent within the committed timeframe, using the template, to the contacts the contract names.
The screening policy sets the checks for each role, the limits the law places on them in each country, the recheck interval for sensitive roles, and that access waits for clearance.
The list of joiners, moves into sensitive roles and contractors with equal access in the period was complete.
Each person selected had a completed and cleared check dated before access to production or customer data was granted.
Contractors with equal access were screened to the same standard, directly or through their employer's contract.
Rechecks for the listed roles happened on time, and results were stored with no more personal detail than needed.

The training plan is approved and sets who must take it, contractors with access included, the topics, the extra modules for roles such as engineers and administrators, the deadline after joining and the yearly repeat.
The training given in the period covered phishing, social engineering, credential handling, data classification and incident reporting, and the role modules reached the roles listed.
Every person on the staff list and every contractor with access completed the yearly training in the period, and each joiner completed it within the set time.
Anyone overdue was reminded and escalated, and the follow up was recorded until the training was done.

Each role has a written description of the qualifications, experience and responsibilities it needs, with a security duties section covering following policy and reporting incidents, plus the extra duties of technical roles.
Every role held by a current member of staff had a description with a security duties section.
The duties in each description matched the controls the role holder owns in the ownership register and the access the role receives.
Descriptions were updated when a role changed materially, and each was reviewed within the last 12 months.

The approved onboarding checklist covers signed agreements, policy acknowledgement, security training due within a set period from the start date, and access requested and approved from the role definition.
Every joiner in the period had an onboarding checklist, checked against the HR list of starters and the accounts created.
Each joiner selected signed the agreements and acknowledged the policies by the dates the checklist sets, with each step recorded separately.
Access for each joiner selected was requested and approved for the role before it was granted, and was not copied from another user.
Each joiner selected completed security training within the set period from the start date.

The approved offboarding checklist covers removing access, returning devices, badges, keys and tokens, rotating shared secrets, handing over accounts, documents and custodian duties, and a reminder of duties that continue, each with a time limit.

The checklist starts from the HR system when employment ends, sets the access removal time in hours for involuntary departures, and is also run for the access, asset and duty items when someone changes role.
Every leaver on the roster for the period had a closed offboarding record, and each role change had the access, asset and duty items run.
Access for each leaver was removed within the set time of the end date on the roster, and within hours for involuntary departures.
For each leaver selected, every item was done and dated by a named person, devices and tokens came back or were wiped, ownership was handed over, and the leaver acknowledged the duties that continue.

Approved templates exist for the staff and contractor confidentiality and IP agreement, the NDA for other outside parties and the contract security clause. Duties survive the end of the engagement, and each template was reviewed in the last 12 months.
The list of staff, contractors and outside parties who started in the period was complete when compared with the joiner roster and the contractor register.
Each person and outside party selected signed the right agreement before receiving confidential information or access.
Each employment contract and contractor agreement selected carried the security clause stating the person's duties, the policies to follow and the consequence of a breach.
Where a person's access scope or the applicable law changed materially, the agreement was refreshed and signed again.
The performance review process sets a review for every employee at least once a year, names who reviews, and includes the security duties of the role in what is assessed.
Every employee in post for the cycle had a completed review in the last 12 months, with the person, the reviewer and the date recorded.
Each review selected assessed the person against the expectations of the role, including its security and control duties.
Skills gaps found in reviews were recorded with a training or development action that was followed up, and review records were kept confidentially by HR.

The contractor procedure requires a sponsor, a signed agreement before access, the same policy, training and access approval steps as employees, a fixed end date, and removal of access and return of devices, badges and data at the end.
Every contractor engaged in the period appeared in the register with company, sponsor, start date, end date and the systems they can reach, and the register matched the accounts held.
Each contractor selected signed the agreement, acknowledged the policies and completed training by the time access began, and that access was approved.
Each contractor who reached the end date lost access on that date unless an extension was approved, and the return of each device, badge and data item was recorded.
Contractor accounts were included in each access review in the period.

The access policy is approved. It requires every in scope application that supports single sign on to sign in through the identity provider, sets second factor and session rules there, and says who approves an exception and what safeguard it needs.
Each dated export in the period listed every in scope application with whether it signs in through single sign on, and the list matched the applications recorded in the vendor register.
Every application outside single sign on had an approved exception with the reason, the safeguard used instead such as a password manager and a second factor, the approver and the date.
For each leaver, disabling the identity provider account removed access to the applications behind it, and access to each application outside single sign on was removed separately.

The access policy is approved and requires a second factor for every user on every system that supports one. It names the factors allowed, asks for phishing resistant factors for administrators and production, and says who approves exceptions.
The identity provider required a second factor for all users throughout the period, and every active user had a factor enrolled.
Every administrator account, including cloud root and break glass accounts, required a second factor, and a phishing resistant one where the system supports it.
Every account without a second factor had an approved exception stating the reason, the safeguard used instead, the approver and an expiry, and no exception ran past its expiry.
Accounts found without an enrolled factor, or with the second factor turned off, were raised as findings and fixed or given an approved exception.

The password policy is approved. It requires at least 12 characters, screening against known breached passwords, single use first and reset passwords, lockout after no more than 10 failed attempts, an identity check before any reset, and no sharing.
The dated password settings at the identity provider matched the policy for minimum length, breached password screening and reuse throughout the period.
Accounts locked after no more than 10 failed attempts, for at least 30 minutes or until the person's identity was confirmed, or sign in was rate limited where lockout was not available.
Passwords were changed when a credential was known or suspected to be exposed, and any scheduled change the settings enforced traced to a contract or rule named in the policy.

The policy is approved and requires shared credentials, and those for applications outside single sign on, to be kept in the company password manager. It names the tool and who manages it, and bans sharing credentials by chat or email.
Each dated member export from the password manager matched the staff list: every active member of staff had an account and no leaver kept one.
Secrets were kept in vaults scoped by team or role rather than one shared vault, and each shared vault had a named owner and members who match the team it serves.
At offboarding each leaver lost vault access, and every shared credential they could read was rotated.

Roles are defined for each job function and approved by the owner of each system. The role and access matrix states, for each role, the systems it reaches and the access level, set at the least the job needs.
In each in scope system, access was given through groups or roles rather than to individuals, and each dated membership export matched the role and access matrix.
Joiners and people who changed job in the period were given access from their role definition, not copied from another user.
Role definitions were reviewed and approved again by their owners at the set interval, and permissions the role no longer needed were removed.

The access request procedure is written and approved. It says how access is requested, who approves for each system, that the system or data owner approves privileged access, and that nothing is granted before the approval is recorded.
The list of access granted in the period was complete for every in scope system, and every joiner of the period appeared on it.
Each grant had a recorded request with a business reason and an approval by the named approver, dated before the access was given.
Privileged grants were approved by the system or data owner, not by the requester's manager alone, and nobody approved their own access.
Each person used an account of their own. Every shared or generic account had an approved exception with a named owner.

The access removal procedure is approved. It sets how fast access is removed after a leaver or role change, in hours for involuntary departures, who removes it and how removal is checked, and covers systems outside single sign on, shared credentials, remote access and code.
The list of leavers for the period matched the HR tool and showed each system every leaver held.
Each leaver's access was removed within the set time of the last working day, and within hours for involuntary departures, with the date and who removed it recorded.
For each leaver and role change, access to systems outside single sign on, shared credentials, remote access and code repositories was removed as well as the identity provider account.
Active accounts were reconciled with active staff at the set interval, and each account without a current owner was investigated and closed or given an owner.
The review procedure is written and approved. It names the systems, the frequency for each class of system and who certifies.
Each review started from a complete account list taken from the system itself on a stated date, including service and outside party accounts.
Reviews took place at the set frequency for every in scope system in the period.
Each account was certified one by one by the system or data owner, and nobody certified their own access.
Access not confirmed was removed or changed within the set time, and the removal was checked.
The privileged access review procedure is written and approved, and states the review frequency and who reviews.
Every privileged account and powerful tool on in scope systems was identified, with its owner, the reason it is needed and the approval of the grant.
Privileged access was reviewed at the defined frequency throughout the period.
Each review covered every in scope system that grants privileged access, checked against the system inventory.
Access found inappropriate was removed, with a traceable record.

The conflicting duties matrix is approved. It lists the duties one person must not hold together, such as deploying and approving the same change or creating and paying a vendor, and the rule or safeguard for each.
Each conflict was separated in system permissions, with maker checker approval where the system supports it, so the person who entered a sensitive action could not also approve it.
Where team size made separation impractical, an approved safeguard such as an independent review of the logged action was in place and was carried out.

Access was checked against the matrix at least once a year, and every quarter for payment and other high risk financial systems, and again when the team grew or was restructured. Each conflict found was fixed or covered by an approved safeguard.

The access policy is approved. It requires each service account, API key and integration token to have an owner, a purpose and the least access it needs, bans default or highly privileged service accounts, and sets the rotation and review intervals.
The inventory listed every service account, API key and integration token in the cloud console, identity provider and build settings, each with an owner, purpose, created date and last rotation date.
No default or highly privileged provider service account was in use, and the permissions of each account were limited to its stated purpose.
Credentials were rotated on the set schedule and at once after any suspected exposure, with the date and who did it recorded.
The inventory was reviewed in the last 12 months, and accounts with no recent sign in activity were disabled or removed.

The session timeout standard is approved. It sets the idle timeout and maximum session length for the product, admin tools and staff applications, with shorter limits for admin interfaces and systems holding sensitive data.
The dated session settings in the identity provider, the cloud console and the product matched the idle timeout and maximum session length in the standard.
Changing second factor settings, granting access and other high risk actions asked the user to sign in again.
Signing out and disabling an account ended active sessions and refresh tokens, not only future sign ins.

The encryption standard is approved. It names every kind of data store that must be encrypted at rest, including databases, object storage, snapshots, backups and disks, the method used, and who manages the keys.
Every data store in the asset inventory had encryption at rest turned on, shown by a dated export from the cloud console that names the key used for each store.
Stores holding data that a contract or regulation names used the key type the standard requires, such as customer managed keys, and every other store used at least provider managed keys.
Stores created in the period were encrypted from the start through policy or infrastructure code, and any store found without encryption was fixed and recorded.

The encryption in transit standard is approved. It sets the minimum TLS version, requires TLS at the edge, between internal services and to databases, and says how certificates are renewed and how old clients are handled.
Every public endpoint accepted only TLS 1.2 or higher with legacy protocols and weak ciphers turned off, shown by a dated scan of each domain and the TLS policy set on the load balancer.
Plain HTTP requests to each public endpoint were redirected to HTTPS and HSTS was set, so a connection could not be pushed down to an unencrypted one.
Traffic between internal services and every database connection required TLS, not only traffic arriving at the edge.
Certificate expiry was monitored and renewal was automated, and no certificate on a public endpoint expired during the period.

The key management policy is approved. It lists the key types, where keys are held apart from the data they protect, who may use and who may manage them, the rotation interval and the steps when a key may be exposed.
Keys were held in a dedicated key service or HSM apart from the data they protect, and the right to use a key and the right to manage it sat with different roles.
Who can use and manage each key was reviewed in the last 12 months, with the date, the reviewer, each key and the changes made.
Each key rotated on the schedule the policy sets, and any key suspected of exposure was rotated at once, with the date recorded.
Retired keys were disabled first and destroyed only once no data or backup still depended on them, with each step recorded.

The secrets management standard is approved. It names the secret store, bans secrets in source code, images and repository files, sets who may read each secret and the rotation interval, and treats an exposed secret as an incident.
Every secret used by in scope services was held in the secret store with a named owner, and the dated list of secrets showed names and dates only, never values.
Each secret was rotated within the interval the standard sets, and each secret found past it was rotated and recorded.
Each secret exposed in the period, such as one found in source code, was rotated at once and handled as an incident.
A dated network diagram, updated with each change and reviewed yearly, shows each trust zone and subnet, the paths allowed between them, the internet entry points and where customer data flows.
Databases and internal services sat in private subnets with no route from the internet, and production was kept apart from development, corporate and guest networks.
The rules between zones were reviewed at least quarterly, with the reviewer, a keep or remove decision for each rule and the changes made.

Separation was tested by trying paths that should be blocked, at least yearly, every six months where it narrows the scope of card data, and after each change to the rules between zones. Each path found open was closed.

The infrastructure standard is approved. It requires inbound traffic to be denied unless a rule allows it, an owner and purpose for every allow rule, where the rule register is kept, and a quarterly review of the rules.
Every firewall and security group denied inbound traffic by default, and each allow rule appeared in the register with its source, destination, port, owner and purpose.
No rule opened a sensitive port to every internet address unless a recorded justification was approved, and each rule without one was removed.
The rules were reviewed at least quarterly. Each review recorded the date, the reviewer, a keep or remove decision for every rule and the changes made, and rules for retired services were removed.

The infrastructure standard is approved. It bars SSH, RDP and database ports from the internet, names the approved route for administrators, such as a session manager, and sets how often the external surface is scanned.
No inbound rule opened an administrative port, such as SSH 22, RDP 3389 or a database port, to the internet, shown by a dated export of every rule open to public ranges.
Each management port left reachable from the internet had an approved exception with the reason, the safeguard used instead, the approver and an expiry date, or a dated nil return was kept.
A change that opened a management port to a public range raised an alert that was investigated, and administrators reached systems only through the approved route.

A written and approved rule requires every public service to sit behind a web application firewall and DDoS protection, sets how new rules move from detection to blocking, and requires the origin to refuse traffic that bypasses them.
Every public service in the asset inventory was fronted by the web application firewall and DDoS protection, with its rules blocking rather than only detecting once tuned.
The origin of each public service refused traffic that did not come through the firewall.
The rules and alerts were reviewed at least quarterly, recording the reviewer, the rules active, the main blocks seen and the changes made, and genuine attack patterns were passed to detection.

The remote access standard is approved. It names the VPN or zero trust tool, requires multi factor sign in and a device check for administrative access, and grants access per application rather than to the whole network.
The remote access tool enforced multi factor sign in and the device rules the standard sets, shown in its dated settings.
Every member of the remote access tool was a current member of staff or an approved contractor, and each leaver was removed.
Access was granted per application, and remote sessions were logged and reviewed together with privileged access.
The threat detection procedure is approved. It names the detection service, who triages its alerts, the response time, and when an alert is raised as an incident.
The detection service was turned on in every cloud account and region in the asset inventory, and turning it off or creating an account without it raised an alert.

Every alert in the period was looked at by a named person who recorded the decision and the date closed within the response time the procedure sets, or a dated nil return with the empty export was kept.
Alerts that met the procedure's incident criteria were raised as incidents and appear in the incident register.
Known benign findings were suppressed only through a recorded tuning decision that gives the reason.

The hardening standard is approved. It names the baseline, such as a CIS benchmark, for each kind of system, including servers, containers, databases, cloud services and network devices, how drift is checked and when baselines are reviewed.
New systems were built from images, infrastructure code or device templates that apply the baseline, with the services and tools a system did not need removed or turned off.
Each system that missed a baseline setting had an approved exception naming the system, the reason, the safeguard used instead, the approver and an expiry date, or a dated nil return was kept.
Drift from the baselines was checked at least quarterly. Each regression found, including network device firmware past its vendor's support, was fixed or covered by an approved exception.
The baselines were reviewed in the last 12 months and again when a new version of the benchmark was released.

The endpoint encryption policy is approved. It requires full disk encryption on every company device, enforced through device management, with recovery keys held centrally and exceptions approved by the security lead.
Every company device in the inventory was encrypted throughout the period, as reported by device management, with its recovery key held centrally.
Encryption was checked before each device was issued and at each periodic compliance check, and devices found unencrypted were fixed.
Each device left unencrypted had an approved exception naming the owner, reason, safeguard used instead, approver and expiry, and no exception ran past its expiry.

The endpoint protection standard is approved. It names the tool, requires it on every managed endpoint and server with automatic updates and removable media scanning, says who handles alerts, and how systems that do not need it are recorded and rechecked.

Every managed endpoint and server ran the agent with current updates, checked against the device and asset inventories, and each one without it was fixed or had a recorded reason rechecked in the last 12 months.
Each endpoint alert in the period was reviewed, with the device, severity, reviewer, action taken and date closed recorded.
Alerts that pointed to a security incident were passed into the incident process and entered in the incident register, rather than left in the product console.

The device management policy is approved. It requires each company device to be enrolled before issue, sets the baseline enforced for encryption, screen lock, patch level and permitted software, covers lost devices, and says if personal devices are enrolled or refused.
Every company device was enrolled in device management, and each was enrolled before it was issued to staff.
Enrolled devices were reconciled with the staff roster, and each person with no managed device or with an unmanaged one was followed up.
The baseline was applied to enrolled devices from the central console, and devices that fell out of it were reported and fixed.

The patch policy is approved. It sets timeframes by severity for operating systems, browsers and installed software on laptops and servers, requires deployment through device management or a patch tool, and says how exceptions are approved.
Patches were deployed automatically through device management or a patch tool rather than left to each user.
Each device and server was patched within the timeframe for the severity, as shown by the monthly reports across the period.
Devices and servers that fell behind were followed up and patched, or given an approved exception.
Critical patches released out of cycle were applied through the emergency change path and reviewed afterwards.

The lost device and leaver procedure is approved. It says how staff report a lost device, who issues the wipe and how fast, how devices that leavers do not return are wiped, and that credentials are rotated when a device never reconnects.
Every managed device could be wiped remotely, as shown by its enrollment in device management.
Each device reported lost or stolen, and each device a leaver did not return, was wiped, checked against the lost device reports and the leaver list.
Each wipe was confirmed as done, not assumed from the command, and the confirmation was kept with the device, owner, reason, date and who did it.
For each device that never reconnected, the credentials it held were rotated and the rotation was recorded.

The screen lock standard is approved. It sets an idle timeout of no more than 15 minutes, requires authentication to unlock, applies to every device type that reaches company data, and is enforced through device management.
Screen lock was enforced by device management on every company device rather than left to user preference, checked against the device inventory.
Every device applied an idle lock time within the standard and asked for authentication to unlock.
Devices found out of line with the standard were fixed, and each fix was recorded.

The classification policy is approved. It sets the levels, how each set of data gets its level, how each level is marked and when marking may be left out, and the storage, sending, sharing and disposal rules for each level.
Every system and data store in the asset inventory carried a classification and an owner, set by its data owner.
Information was marked with its level by the method the policy sets, such as a header, metadata tag or sensitivity label, in the documents, email, files and system records sampled.
Staff were trained during the period on the classification scheme and how to mark information, and the acceptable use policy refers to it.

Approved policy requires a data map covering databases, object storage, file shares, analytics platforms and vendor systems, sets what is recorded for each store, and requires a refresh each year and when systems or vendors are added.
Each data store in the map recorded its data categories, classification, owner, location, retention period and protections such as encryption, access model and backup treatment.
The map showed where data flows into and out of each store, including to and from vendor systems.

In the last 12 months and when systems or vendors were added, a dated review compared the map with the cloud console, app list and vendor register, recorded stores added or removed, and was signed off.

The retention schedule is approved. It sets for each data type how long it is kept, why, the legal need, how it is deleted, which records must stay unaltered for their period, and how a legal hold starts and ends.

Data past its retention period was deleted by a lifecycle rule, expiry setting or scheduled purge job, and the deletion records show the data type, date range, run date, what ran it and record counts.
Backups, archives and analytics copies were deleted on the same schedule as the primary stores, within the backup retention window stated in the backup policy.
Each legal hold in the period was documented with the data it covered and its start date, suspended deletion for that data only, and was lifted when the hold ended.

The disposal procedure is approved. It covers every copy of data, including replicas, indexes, caches, analytics, vendor systems and backups, and retired devices and media, with approved methods, sign off and records kept.
Every device and medium retired, sold, returned or reissued in the period had a disposal record with item, serial number, method, date and who did it, or a dated nil return was kept.
Each method fitted the data the item held, the result was confirmed before reuse or disposal, and a certificate was kept for each item a disposal contractor handled.
Data deleted in the period was removed from every copy the data map lists, including indexes, caches, analytics and vendor systems, and aged out of backups within the stated window.

Approved policy bars production data from development and test, names the approved way to make test data, such as masked, synthetic or subset data, and requires approval, a time limit and a reason for any production restore.
Lower environments in the period were filled by the approved seed or masking method, and test records showed fake or masked values.
Data sets in lower environments were checked during the period for data that looks like production personal data, and any found was removed and recorded.
The privacy notice is approved, versioned and dated. It states what is collected, why, the legal basis, who receives it, how long it is kept, the rights people hold and how to get in touch.
The notice matched practice: its data, purposes, recipients and retention periods agreed with the data map, purpose register, disclosure register and retention schedule.
Every version published in the period was kept with its date and what changed, or a dated note shows the notice did not change.
Each material change was announced through the channel the notice commits to before it took effect.

The procedure is approved. Where consent is the basis, it is asked for per purpose, explicitly for sensitive data, is as easy to withdraw as to give, and each record keeps the time, purpose, notice version and capture method.
Each consent relied on in the period had a record with the person or ID, the date, the purpose agreed, the notice version shown and how it was captured.
Where sensitive categories of data were collected on the basis of consent, the record showed an explicit agreement for that purpose, given before collection.
Each withdrawal in the period was acted on promptly, processing for that purpose stopped and the withdrawal reached downstream systems and processors, or a dated nil return was kept.

The procedure is approved. It links every collection point to a stated purpose, has new fields questioned at design review, keeps personal data out of logs, error trackers and analytics events, and sets a yearly field review.
In the last 12 months each form, API and import that collects personal data was reviewed, with the fields collected and why each is needed, and fields that served no purpose were removed.
Each new field collecting personal data added in the period was questioned at design review before release, with the reason it is needed recorded.

The purpose register and procedure are approved. They list each type of personal data with its purpose and legal basis, require approval before any new use, and state the position on using customer or personal data to train AI models.
Access to personal data was limited to the roles whose purpose in the register needs it.
Each new use of personal data in the period was approved before it started and fell under a purpose in the privacy notice, or the notice was updated first, or a dated nil return was kept.
No customer or personal data was used to train AI models beyond the stated position, and each such use was approved and recorded.
In the last 12 months actual data flows were compared with the stated purposes, and each difference was resolved and recorded.

The access request procedure is approved. It names a single intake point, the deadline set by the law that applies, how identity is checked, who answers, and that each answer covers every system holding the data and the disclosures made.

Every access request received in the period was logged with date received, type, identity check, date answered and outcome, including those that arrived outside the intake point, or a dated nil return was kept.
Each request was answered within the deadline, and the requester's identity was confirmed before any data was disclosed.
Each sampled answer drew on every system in the data map that held the person's data and listed the third parties their data went to.

The correction procedure is approved. It says how people ask for a correction, how identity is checked, who makes the change, the deadline, and how processors, third parties and backups are updated within a set window.
Each correction made in the period followed an identity check that fitted the data involved, recorded before the change was made.
Each correction was made within the deadline, and the third parties and processors holding the data were told, with the date of each notice, or a dated nil return was kept.
Personal data held in more than one system was compared during the period, and each difference found was corrected and recorded.

The procedure is approved. It routes every new flow of personal data to a third party through vendor review and approval, and keeps a register of each recipient, the data, the purpose and the legal basis, reviewed yearly.
Every third party that received personal data in the period was in the register with the data shared, the purpose and the lawful basis or consent relied on.
Each disclosure that started in the period had a recorded basis, approver and date before data was first sent, and matched the privacy notice and any consent given, or a dated nil return was kept.
In the last 12 months the register was compared with the systems actually sending personal data, such as integrations and vendor connections, and each difference was corrected.

The personal data handling procedure is approved. It requires every unauthorized disclosure and near miss to be recorded, notifiable or not, with the data and people affected, the cause, the containment and the notice decision with its reason.

Every unauthorized disclosure and near miss in the period was in the register, including those judged not notifiable, and each privacy incident in the incident register appeared in it, or a dated nil return was kept.
Each entry recorded the date, what was disclosed and to whom, the data categories, the number of people affected, how it was found, the cause, the containment and whether notice was given.
The register was reviewed during the period for repeated causes, and each pattern found led to a recorded action with an owner.

The supplier policy is approved and requires a data processing agreement with every vendor that processes personal data, covering permitted purposes, security duties, subprocessing, breach notice, deletion and audit rights.
Every vendor in the register that handles personal data had a signed data processing agreement on file, with its version and the date signed.
Each signed agreement covered permitted purposes, security duties, subprocessing, breach notice, deletion and audit rights, or the missing term was recorded and tracked.
Where a vendor relationship or the law that applies changed in the period, the agreement was reviewed and signed again or recorded as still adequate.
The supplier policy is approved and requires every data processing agreement to carry a breach notice clause with a timeframe in hours and the content the first notice must hold.
Each vendor with a data processing agreement had its breach notice timeframe in hours, and where the clause sits in the contract, recorded in the vendor register.
The notification contact path for each critical vendor was tested or confirmed current at the vendor's last review.

Each vendor breach notice received in the period was logged with date received, the impact, the action and date closed, and led to a notice decision of the company's own, or a dated nil return was kept.

The breach notification procedure is approved. It sets what makes an incident notifiable to regulators, customers and affected people, the deadline under each law and contract that applies, who decides, and holds templates cleared by legal in advance.

Every incident in the period that touched personal or customer data carried a recorded notice decision with its reason and who decided, including decisions not to notify, or a dated nil return matched the incident register.
Each notice that was due went to the right regulator, customers or affected people within the deadline that applied, using the approved templates, and a copy of each notice sent was kept.

The deadlines and recipients in the procedure were checked in the last 12 months against the countries of operation and the notice terms in customer contracts, and the templates were updated where they had changed.

The procedure is approved. It names the privacy contact point, routes it to a tracked queue with an owner rather than one person's mailbox, and sets the response time, escalation and how outcomes are logged.
The privacy contact point was published in the privacy notice and on the website throughout the period, and messages sent to it reached the tracked queue.
Each inquiry and complaint in the period was logged with date received, topic, date resolved and outcome, and was resolved within the set time or escalated, or a dated nil return was kept.
Complaints in the period were reviewed for common causes, and each cause found led to a recorded action.
A standard requires review by someone other than the author before merge for every in scope repository and defines the allowed exceptions.
Every repository holding production code was identified and in scope, and each exclusion had a recorded reason.
Each in scope repository enforced review on its default branch throughout the period, with direct pushes blocked, at least one approval required and bypass limited.
Every change merged in the period was approved before merge by someone other than its author.
Each bypass or emergency merge was recorded and reviewed afterwards.

The testing standard is approved. It names the tests and checks that must pass before a change merges, requires tests of processing accuracy and completeness where the system handles customer data, and says how the CI settings enforce the gate.
Each in scope repository required the named checks to pass before merge on its default branch, set in branch protection so that no individual could skip them.
Every change merged in the period ran the required checks and passed them before merge, shown on a complete list of merges with commit, checks, result and run date kept for the whole period.
Merges made with a required check failed, skipped or overridden were found, and each was explained and reviewed or raised as a finding.
Where the system processes customer data, the suite held tests that confirm processing is accurate and complete, and those tests ran among the required checks.

The environment design is approved. It shows development, staging and production in separate accounts or projects with separate credentials and data, the order changes are promoted in, and who may reach each environment.
Production ran in its own cloud accounts or projects, apart from development and staging, as shown by the account list for the period.
Only people and roles with an approved need could reach production, checked against the production access list and the privileged access approvals.
Changes reached production through the set sequence of environments, and none was deployed straight to production outside it.
Development and staging held no production data, only masked or synthetic data, and were protected by their own access control.

The change management policy is approved. It says what counts as a change, including database, configuration, infrastructure and server software, who approves, the testing and rollback needed before release, and how emergency and standard changes work.
Every production change released in the period appeared on the change list, checked against the changes merged and deployed to production.
Each change was authorized and approved before release, and its record stated the expected impact, the testing done and how it would be rolled back.
Deployments that reached production without a linked approved change were found and investigated, and the outcome was recorded.
Changes released as standard changes fell within a standard change approved in advance, and each standard change was reviewed in the last 12 months.

The emergency change procedure is approved. It says when a change counts as an emergency, who may authorize one, what must be recorded at the time, and that a review and approval follows within a set window, normally the next business day.
Every change released through the emergency route in the period was identified, checked against the merges made without the normal review.
Each emergency change was authorized by a person the procedure allows, and its reason and the actions taken were recorded at the time.
Each emergency change was reviewed and approved afterwards, within the set window, by someone other than the person who made it.
The number and causes of emergency changes were reviewed at management review, and a rising rate led to action on the normal change path.

The secure development policy is approved. It covers design review, code review, testing, environments and release, lists the design principles new systems follow, sets secure coding, code analysis, dependency and secrets rules, and names an owner for each step.

Each new application, major feature and acquired system in the period had its security requirements recorded and approved at design review before it was built or bought, and checked as met before release.
Design reviews or threat models for work in the period recorded the security risks considered, the decisions made and the reviewer.
Everyone who wrote or reviewed code completed secure coding training when they joined and again in the last 12 months.
The engineering lead reviewed the policy in the last 12 months against the tooling actually in use, and the review was recorded.

The deployment procedure is approved. It says who and what may deploy to production, that releases come only from the protected default branch or a pipeline build, the approval needed before a deployment runs, and how rollback works.
Every production deployment in the period came from the protected default branch or from a release the pipeline built.
Each production deployment was approved, or ran through a protected environment with named reviewers, before it started.
Only the listed people and pipeline identities could deploy to production, and deployment credentials were held in the pipeline rather than on laptops.
The deployment history for the period was complete, showing what was released, from which commit, when, and by whom or what.

The change procedure is approved. It requires every production change to reference a ticket, its pull request to link to that ticket and its release to the commit, says where the approver is recorded, and sets retention of at least 12 months.
Every change released in the period referenced a ticket, and its pull request and release were linked to that ticket.
The approver of each change was recorded on its ticket or pull request.
Tickets and pull requests for released changes were kept for at least 12 months, or longer where the audit period or the retention schedule requires it.
A sample of changes was traced each quarter from request to release, and each break in the trail was followed up.

The dependency triage standard is approved. It names the scanner for code dependencies and container images, sets triage and fix timeframes by severity, says which new critical findings fail a build and how exceptions are approved, and requires a component list with licenses.
Dependency and image scanning ran on every in scope repository and image registry in the period, checked against the asset inventory.
Builds that introduced a new critical vulnerability failed rather than only reporting it, and any release made despite one had an approved exception.
Each dependency and image alert was triaged within the timeframe for its severity, with the date found, date triaged, decision and due date recorded.
Alerts were fixed by their due date or carried as an approved exception with a reason and expiry, and overdue alerts were raised as findings.

The exposed secret procedure is approved. It requires secret scanning on every repository, including full history, and pre commit hooks, says who is told when a secret leaks and how fast it is rotated, and how use of the old secret is checked.
Secret scanning, including full commit history, was turned on for every in scope repository throughout the period.
Every exposed secret found in the period was rotated within the time the procedure sets, with the date found and the date rotated recorded.
For each exposed secret, use of the credential before rotation was investigated and the conclusion was recorded.
Each exposure was handled as a security incident and entered in the incident register.

The input validation standard is approved. It requires every API, form and data feed to check schema, type, length, range and required fields at the boundary, names the library used, and says how duplicates and rejected records are handled.
Validation at the system boundary was tested in the period by automated tests, a scanner or the penetration test, and the results show what was tested, the method and the outcome.
Input validation weaknesses found by those tests were fixed and retested, or carried as an accepted risk with an owner.
Duplicate and invalid records were caught at ingestion and sent to a monitored queue rather than dropped, and rejection rates above the expected level raised an alert that was followed up.
Each key data flow has an approved processing specification stating its inputs, data definitions, steps and calculation logic, outputs, accuracy rules, error handling and processing time commitments.
Each specification was versioned with its system, and the version in force matched the processing running in production.
Test cases for processing logic referred to the specification, so that they checked the stated behaviour rather than whatever the code did.
Every change to processing logic in the period was matched by a review of the specification, recording the reviewer, the date and the approved updated version.

The reconciliation procedure is approved. It names each job and what is compared, such as record counts and control totals between source and destination, how often, the tolerance, and who handles mismatches.
Job runs were monitored for success, failure and runs that did not start, and each missed or failed run was detected and followed up.
Each run in the period was reconciled between source and destination as the procedure sets, and the results were kept.
Each break beyond tolerance raised an alert and was investigated before any reprocessing, and its cause and fix were recorded.

The pipeline design is approved. For each stage it shows where data is stored, that the store is durable and versioned, the checksum or record count check between stages, and what happens when a check fails.
Integrity checks ran between stages throughout the period, and each run recorded the checks made and whether they passed.
Each failed integrity check was acted on as the design says, and the action and its outcome were recorded.
Intermediate data was held in durable, versioned storage, and stages that were retried did not duplicate or lose records.
Intermediate data was kept no longer than the processing specification and the retention schedule allow, and was deleted when that time ran out.

The logging and retention standard is approved. It names the systems that send logs, the events logged, the central store, who may read and who may delete logs, and how long logs are kept and searchable.
Sign in, access change, administrator and application audit events from every in scope system reached the central log store, and a source that stopped sending raised an alert.
Logs were kept for at least 12 months with the latest 3 months searchable at once, and the administrators of a system could not change or delete its logs.
Security events were reviewed at least daily by alert rules or a person, and each monthly review record gave the reviewer, the sources covered, what was found and what was done.

The asset management policy is approved. It says which kinds of asset are listed, the details kept for each, such as owner and classification, the sources the list is built from and how often it is reviewed.
Every asset in service was listed with its type, owner, classification and status, and each owner was an active member of the workspace.
The inventory was complete. Resources found in connected cloud, identity and device sources, and the systems of listed vendors, all appeared in it.
The inventory was reviewed at least quarterly, with the reviewer, the sources compared, the assets added or retired, and a sign off recorded.

The alerting standard is approved. It lists the security conditions that raise alerts, drawn from identity, cloud, endpoint and application logs, where each alert goes, its severity and the response time.
Alerts covered the priority conditions: unauthorized access attempts, unusual sign ins, privilege escalation, unusual outbound traffic, changes to critical files, outages and resource exhaustion.
Each alert had an owner and a defined first response, and alerts nobody acted on were removed.
Alert volume and false alarms were reviewed at least quarterly, recording the reviewer, the noisy or missing alerts, the rules changed and the reason for each change.
The escalation policy is written and approved. It names who is paged first, when an unanswered page escalates and to whom, and the acknowledgement and response times for each severity.
Someone was on call for every day of the period with a backup and contact details, including nights and weekends where commitments require it.
Security and availability alerts were routed to the rotation through a tool that escalates unacknowledged pages as the escalation policy sets.
Missed and unacknowledged pages were tracked and reviewed, and gaps in cover were fixed.

The vulnerability management policy is approved. It sets the scan scope and frequency, the fix timeframe for each severity, how findings from every source enter one register, and how a risk acceptance is approved.

Infrastructure, containers, dependencies and the external surface were scanned at least quarterly and after significant change, with authenticated scans on internal systems, and the targets matched the asset inventory.
Every finding was recorded in the register with its severity, asset, owner and due date, including findings from penetration tests and bug reports.
Findings were fixed within the timeframe for their severity, and performance against the timeframes was measured.
Each finding not fixed in time had a documented risk acceptance, approved as the policy sets.

An approved configuration baseline sets the expected settings for servers, cloud accounts and services, with a version and approval date, and names the high risk regressions that alert at once and how each is fixed.
Cloud configuration was monitored continuously against the baseline, and high risk regressions such as public storage, logging turned off or an opened management port raised an alert.
Each drift alert was investigated and closed with its cause and the action taken, within the time set for its type, or a dated nil return with the empty export was kept.
Drift that recurred was traced to its cause in how systems are provisioned, and that cause was fixed.
The triage procedure is approved. It sets the severity levels and the criteria for each, who decides whether an event is an incident, and the escalation path and response time for each severity.
Every security event in the period was evaluated and the decision recorded with the date, source and evaluator, including events judged benign, or a dated nil return with the empty queue was kept.
Events judged to be incidents were escalated as the procedure sets for their severity and appear in the incident register.
Triage decisions were reviewed for consistency, and events found to be misclassified were corrected.

The incident response plan is approved. It sets severity levels, roles, the steps from detection to closure, who must be told for each kind of incident with the notice decision as a set step, and how evidence is collected and kept.
A current list names the incident lead and backups, legal, communications and the support routes of key vendors, with phone and email for each.
The plan was shared with everyone who holds a role in it, and was reviewed in the last 12 months and after each significant incident.
Every security incident in the period was recorded with date found, severity, owner, the notice decision and date closed, or a signed nil return was kept.
Incidents were handled as the plan says. Each severity matched the plan's levels, and the notice decision was made and recorded within the time the plan sets.

The incident response plan and corrective action procedure are approved. They require a blameless postmortem for each significant incident, set what it records, and say how its actions are owned and tracked.
Each significant incident in the register had a postmortem recording the timeline, impact, root cause and detection gap, or a dated nil return matched the register.
Each corrective action had a named owner and due date and was tracked to closure, and overdue actions were followed up.
Recurring themes across incidents were reviewed, and the lessons were fed back into the plan or the controls.
The incident response plan is approved and requires at least one tabletop exercise a year against a realistic scenario, names who must take part, and says how the results and actions are recorded.
A tabletop exercise was held in the last 12 months against a realistic scenario, and its report records the date, the scenario, the decisions made and the gaps found.
The people who would respond took part, including engineering, leadership and communications.
Each gap found, notably in contacts, access and decision authority, became an action with an owner and due date that was tracked to closure, or the report states that no actions were raised.

Recovery procedures are approved for each key system. They cover restoring from backup, rebuilding a compromised system and rotating affected credentials, who does each step, and when recovery counts as complete.
Each incident that needed recovery had a record of the systems restored, the steps taken and the time to recover, or a dated nil return matched the incident register.
Before service was restored, the system or backup was checked so a compromise was not brought back, and affected credentials were rotated.
Recovery was declared complete only when the procedure's criteria were met, and the confirmation was recorded.

The continuity and recovery plan is approved. It sets recovery time and data loss targets for each critical service, the redundancy each relies on, activation criteria, roles, and how customers and staff are told.

The plan names each critical dependency, third parties included, with a workaround that keeps access control, logging and encryption in place, or names who may approve a temporary relaxation, what compensates and when it ends.
The plan was tested in the last 12 months, including failover of the redundant parts, with the scenario, who took part and the results compared with each recovery target.
Where a secondary site or region exists, the test switched to it and confirmed that access control, logging and segmentation worked there.
Issues found in the test were tracked to closure, and the plan was updated after the test and after each significant change to the architecture.

The operations policy is approved. It lists the resources watched, such as compute, storage, bandwidth, database connections, quotas and licenses, sets alert thresholds below the point of failure, and requires a capacity review at least every quarter.
Capacity was reviewed every quarter, with the date, the reviewer, the use of each resource against its limit and the growth forecast.
Alerts fired at thresholds that left time to act, and no limit was reached in the period without an earlier warning.
Each shortfall a review found led to a recorded change, such as scaling up or raising a quota, with the reason, date and who made it, or the review stated that none was needed.

The backup policy is approved. It names the data stores and the configuration, code and images needed to rebuild each service, and sets frequency and retention from the data loss target, encryption, a separate copy and who monitors.
Every production data store in the asset inventory had automated backups running at the set frequency and retention throughout the period.
Each failed or late backup job raised an alert and a ticket, with the cause, the fix and the date of the next good backup recorded.
Backups were encrypted at rest, restore rights were held by a small reviewed group, and at least one copy sat in a separate region, account or site on immutable or offline storage.

The continuity plan is approved. It sets recovery time and data loss targets, a full restore test at least once a year and after significant change to the data platform, and a quarterly sample restore where backups are on tape or on premises.
A full restore from backup was done in the last 12 months and after each significant change to the data platform, with the date, what was restored, the steps and who did it recorded.
Each test restored into an isolated environment and checked that the data was complete and intact, not only that the job finished.
Each test measured the actual restore time and data loss against the targets, and each missed target led to a recorded action.
Issues found in each test were recorded and tracked to closure.
The supplier policy is approved. It says what the vendor register holds for each vendor, how it is checked for unlisted vendors, and that it is reviewed at least once a year.
Every vendor in use was listed with a business owner who is an active member, the service it provides, the data it can reach and a criticality tier.
The register was complete. Vendors found in payments, in apps connected to the identity provider and among third party assets all appeared in it.
Contract dates and renewal points were recorded, and the register was reviewed in the last 12 months, with vendors no longer used removed and their access revoked.
A supplier procedure sets assessment depth by tier, the contract terms required, the reassessment interval and who decides.
