The vendor register was complete: every supplier with access to systems or data was listed with a tier and an owner.
Each critical or high vendor was assessed before use and again within its tier interval.

For each critical vendor the current assurance report was read: its scope and period cover the services used, exceptions were assessed, the controls it expects of customers are operated, and its own key suppliers are noted.
Contracts carried the agreed security terms, and findings or accepted risks from assessments were tracked to closure.

The cloud services and acceptable use policies are approved. They require new software to go through the vendor process and name where unapproved applications are looked for: identity provider sign ins and grants, expenses and card spend.

Each review in the period checked the applications connected to the identity provider and office suite, expense reports and the single sign on app list, and recorded the date, reviewer and each new application found.
Each new application found was approved and added to the vendor register, or marked for removal, with the reason, who decided and the date.
Approved applications were onboarded with an owner and a tier, and those marked for removal lost their access and grants by the next review.

The subprocessor list is kept in the vendor register and published where customer commitments require. It records each subprocessor's service, the data processed, its location and the last updated date, and the supplier policy sets the notice process.
The published list matched the vendors that actually received customer or personal data, checked against the data map and the vendor register.

Each subprocessor added or changed in the period was announced to customers before use as the contract requires, with the date sent, who was told and the objection period, or a dated nil note was kept.
The published list was updated after each change in the period, so its last updated date is no older than the latest change.

The cloud services policy names the hosting providers relied on for physical security, the kinds of independent assurance accepted, the oldest report period allowed, and who reviews each report every year.
A current report or certificate was obtained for each provider in the last 12 months, and its period, regions and services covered what the company actually uses.
The reviewer read the exceptions and exclusions in the report, assessed each one, and recorded the review with their name, the date and any issue raised.
Each control the provider expects of its customers was matched to a control the company runs, and none was left without an owner.
The reliance on each provider, and which controls it performs, was written into the system description and the statement of applicability.

The office physical access policy is approved. It sets who may enter, how badges or keys are issued, visitor and secure area rules, how unauthorized entry is detected, removal at leaving, and keeping access records at least 90 days.
Each quarter the badge list was compared with the staff list, and the badges of people who had left were removed at offboarding.
Every visitor was logged with name, company, host, date and time in and out, and was escorted in secure areas.
Unauthorized entry was detected by alarms or cameras alerting a named responder, or by recorded building monitoring, and alarm events and access exceptions were reviewed each quarter.
A walk through each quarter checked desks, printers and secure areas, and each issue found, such as an unlocked screen or papers left out, was fixed.

The scope statement names the products, services, cloud environments, sites, teams, systems and data the security program covers, says what is left out and why, and carries leadership's written approval with a date.

The scope explains where it stops by pointing to the factors register and to what interested parties require, lists the suppliers, group companies and outsourced services it relies on, and a data flow diagram shows where sensitive data leaves the covered area.
A map of the management processes names each one, such as risk assessment, internal audit, management review and corrective action, with its owner, what it takes in and what it hands to the next.
Each new product, site or supplier in the period was followed by a dated scope review that recorded whether the scope changed and who approved the result.
The scope was reviewed in the last 12 months, the current approved version was the one in use, and staff, customers and auditors who needed it could reach it.

The factors register lists the outside pressures on the security program, such as law, customers, threats, suppliers and the market, and the inside ones, such as strategy, growth, staffing, technology and budget, with how each affects security and a named owner.
The register records a decision on whether climate change matters to the company, for example through its sites, hosting regions, suppliers or customers, with the reason either way.

The owner and leadership reviewed the register in the last 12 months and after each major event, such as a funding round, an acquisition, a new market, a new law or a serious incident, and recorded what was added or changed.
The factors were used in the risk assessment, the security objectives and the scope, and each action or decision a factor led to was recorded.

The register lists each party with a stake in security, such as customers, regulators, staff, suppliers, investors and insurers, what each expects, including on climate change, whether that is legal, contractual or other, and where it came from.
For each expectation the register says whether the security program takes it on, and every legal and contractual one taken on appears in the obligations register with a named owner.
The register was reviewed in the last 12 months and after each change of a major customer, regulator or contract, and the review recorded what was checked and what changed.
Each new contract term or regulatory change found in the period was added to the register, and those taken on reached the obligations register with an owner.
The objectives plan is approved and sets a small number of measurable security objectives for the year, each traced to the security policy, a risk result or a customer commitment.
Each objective has an owner, a target, a due date and the people, time and budget it needs, and its measure says what is counted, how, how often and who reviews the numbers.
Results were taken each quarter for every objective and compared with its target, and an action with an owner was raised for each one off track.
Leadership reviewed the results at management review and recorded its decisions on people, tools and budget for security, including requests turned down and why.
The objectives were shared with the people working toward them, and any objective that no longer fitted was updated or retired with a recorded reason.

The statement of applicability lists every control in the reference set, plus any added from laws, contracts or other sources, and records for each whether it applies, whether it is in place and who owns it.
Every included and every excluded control gives a specific reason that points to a risk, a legal or contractual requirement or the scope, never a general statement.
Each control chosen in the risk treatment plan appeared as included, and no excluded control was one that a risk in the register depends on.
Each control marked as inherited named the supplier that performs it and was backed by a current certificate or report whose scope covered the service used.

Each version was approved by the risk owners and leadership before use, every approved version was kept, and the statement was reviewed in the last 12 months and reissued when risk treatment or scope changed.
The document control procedure is approved and says how documents are written, approved by a named person, versioned, shared, reviewed at least yearly, kept and withdrawn.
A list names every document and record the program needs, including those the standards, laws and contracts followed call for and the operating procedures for in scope systems, each with an owner.
The document store limits reading and editing by role, keeps version history and backups, and applies retention and disposal periods that meet legal and contractual terms.
Every controlled document carried a title, version, date, owner and next review date, and each version published in the period was approved by its named approver first.
No document was past its review date, superseded versions were withdrawn from use, and outside documents the program relies on, such as supplier reports, were identified and kept current.

The operating plan lists each recurring security activity with its owner, schedule and expected record, and says what counts as done for each, such as scope, method and approver. It is reviewed at least once a year.
Each activity due in the period was done by its owner by the due date and links to the record it left, and each slip has a reason and a new date.
Completed activities met the standard the plan sets for them, with the stated scope, method and approver.

Before each change to the management system or the services in scope, the reason, expected effect, owner, timing and resources were recorded and approved, and unplanned changes were reviewed afterwards for harm.
Security work done by suppliers, contractors or group entities was listed, the standard it must meet was set in the contract or service agreement, and it was checked at the supplier review.

The improvement procedure says how anyone raises an improvement, the sources it draws on, such as audits, incidents, measures, management review, customers and staff, who decides and how accepted items are tracked.
Improvement items from audits, incidents, measurement results and management review in the period all reached the log.
Each item in the log was assessed for benefit and effort and has a recorded decision and reason, and each accepted item has an owner and a due date.
Accepted items were closed only with evidence that the change was made, and items past their due date were followed up.
In the last 12 months a sample of completed improvements was checked at management review for the intended effect, and any follow up was recorded.

The roles with security duties are listed, such as security lead, administrators, on call responders, internal auditors and risk owners, and each has written skill, experience and qualification requirements built on its job description.
The list of security roles covered everyone who held security duties in the period, compared with the role descriptions and the control ownership register.
Each person in a security role had a competence record made before taking up the role and updated in the last 12 months, showing how they meet each requirement and any gap.
Each gap found was given an action such as training, mentoring, supervision or a change of assignment, with a date, and was checked afterwards to confirm it worked.

The security communication plan is approved. For each topic, such as policy changes, incidents, threats, audit results and customer commitments, it states the audience, the timing or trigger, the channel and the sender, inside and outside the company.
The list of security messages for the period was complete, and each topic the plan schedules reached its audience on time through the planned channel.
Messages the plan requires after an event, such as an incident, were sent by the named sender to staff, customers, suppliers or authorities as the plan states.
The plan was reviewed in the last 12 months, and whether messages were received and understood was checked through acknowledgements or feedback.

The contact list is approved. It names the regulators, cyber agencies, police and provider support that may be needed, with contact details, when to contact each, any legal deadline, who may make contact, and who must agree first.
The company belonged to or subscribed to security groups and advisory feeds that fit its technology and sector, and a named person followed each one and passed on what mattered.
In the last 12 months, and after any change of regulator, jurisdiction or site, each contact channel was checked to still work, with the date, who checked and the result recorded.
Each contact with an authority in the period was logged with its date, reason and outcome, and the incident lead and legal counsel agreed to it first unless life or safety was at risk.

The threat source routine is approved. It lists the sources followed and why each was chosen, who reads them and how often, at least weekly, and requires urgent alerts to be assessed on the day they arrive.
The sources were read on schedule, and each relevant item was logged with its assessment, the action taken, an owner and a date, or a dated nil return listed the sources checked.
Each actively exploited vulnerability in software in use was assessed on the day it was published or found, and the days from publication to fix were recorded for each.
Confirmed threats fed the risk assessment and vulnerability priorities, and leadership received a summary of threat trends at each management review.
The choice of sources was reviewed in the last 12 months.

The masking standard is approved. It lists the fields to mask from the classification, checked against the privacy, sector and card rules that apply, the method for each use, where masking is the default and who may see unmasked data.
Masking rules were kept in reviewed code or configuration, and each change to them in the period was approved and recorded.
Every data set used for test, support, analytics, logs or demos in the period was listed with its owner and masking method, and the sample showed the listed fields masked.
Only approved roles could see unmasked data, and card numbers showed no more than the issuer prefix and last four digits to roles that do not need the full number.
In the last 12 months and after each schema or data type change, masked data was tested for reversal by combining fields or reading a mapping, and the result was recorded.

Approved rules list the routes data can leave by from systems holding confidential or restricted data, set the blocks, limits and warnings for each that fit the classification, who may change them and the alert triage time.
Sharing limits and leak alerts, including alerts for bulk downloads and public links, were on in the email, file, chat and cloud storage tools in use, matching the recorded settings.
Removable storage was blocked or restricted on company devices through device management, with encrypted media allowed only by approved exception.
Each leak alert in the period was triaged within the set time and each confirmed leak was raised as an incident, or a dated nil return with the empty report was kept.
Exceptions and rule tuning were reviewed at least every quarter, and the outcome of each review was recorded.

The time source standard is approved. It names the trusted time sources, how servers, containers, devices and managed services use them, the time zone used in log timestamps and the largest clock offset allowed.
Every in scope system took its time only from the recorded trusted sources, including new images, devices and accounts built in the period.
Clock offset was checked at least quarterly across the in scope systems. Each offset was within the allowed limit, or it raised an alert that was followed up.
Log timestamps from every source used one time zone, normally UTC, or carried an explicit offset, so events lined up into one timeline.

The web filtering standard is approved. It lists the blocked or restricted categories, such as malware, phishing, newly registered domains and unapproved file sharing, the tool used, how exceptions are granted, and a coverage review at least quarterly.
The filter covered every managed device in the office and when remote, including each newly enrolled device, checked against the device inventory.
Servers and administrative workstations for card data or other high value systems had no general web access and reached only named update and service destinations.
Each exception was requested and approved with a reason and an end date, and expired exceptions were removed at each review.
Coverage, blocked activity and open exceptions were reviewed at least quarterly, the review was recorded, and repeat hits led to changes in the rules or the training.

The site protection standard is approved. It lists each site the organization runs that holds equipment or information, names an owner for each, and requires a hazard assessment at least once a year and after any change to the site.

Each site's assessment from the last 12 months covered fire, flood, heat, power loss and tampering, and the protections fitted, such as detection, locked racks, backup power, cooling and protected cabling, matched the hazards found.

Site equipment was serviced at the set intervals by approved engineers, supervised in secure areas, storage was removed or wiped before equipment left for repair, and each fault and visit was recorded.
Power failover, alarms and suppression were tested in the last 12 months and each failed test was followed up, or for a shared managed building the landlord's current certificates were kept.

Where payment devices are used, each was listed with location and serial number, inspected for tampering on the set schedule, and site staff were trained to report tampering, or a dated note shows none are used.
